title: Delete one extra “p”.
before:
appple juice
orange juice
lemon tea
after:
apple juice
orange juice
lemon tea
hint: You’re already on the extra letter. In Normal mode, x deletes the character under the cursor.
why: x makes a tiny deletion without leaving Normal mode. No selection, no backspace, no mode switch.

title: Change “cat” to “bat”.
hint: Press r, then the replacement letter.
why: r replaces exactly one character and returns straight to Normal mode.

title: Put “hello ” before “world”.
hint: i enters Insert mode. Type hello followed by a space, then Escape.
why: i inserts before the cursor. Escape brings you back to Normal mode, ready for your next command.

title: Add “!” at the end.
hint: Capital A moves to the end of the line and enters Insert mode.
why: A combines a motion and a mode switch. Use it when you already know the edit belongs at the end.

title: Add a task between these two lines.
after:
make coffee
water the plants
start work
hint: Lowercase o opens a new line below the current one.
why: o creates the line and puts you in Insert mode in one move.

title: Delete “very ”.
hint: w jumps to the next word. Then dw deletes a word and its following space.
why: Think “next word, delete word.” Word motions beat tapping the arrow keys.

title: Delete the first three words.
hint: A count can go between an operator and its motion: d3w.
why: d3w means delete across three word motions. Counts let a single instruction cover a larger distance.

title: Change the first comma to a colon.
hint: f followed by a character finds its next occurrence on the same line.
why: f, lands directly on the comma. rb would replace it with b; here r: makes it a colon.

title: Delete the comment.
hint: Capital D deletes from the cursor through the end of the line. Keep the space before the cursor.
why: D is the compact form of d$. Both express the same edit: delete to the end.

title: Put “# ” at the start.
hint: Capital I starts inserting at the first nonblank character.
why: I takes you to the start of the content, regardless of where you were on the line.

title: Change “cold” to “hot”.
hint: ciw changes the word you’re inside, even if you aren’t on its first letter.
why: Operator + text object: c means change, iw means inner word. The cursor can be anywhere inside the word.

title: Change the text inside the quotes.
hint: ci" changes everything inside the quotes while keeping the quotes.
why: Text objects describe what to edit. ci" saves you from counting characters or locating both ends.

title: Empty the parentheses.
hint: di( deletes inside the surrounding parentheses.
why: The inner object keeps its delimiters. The same pattern works with brackets and braces.

title: Remove “(optional)”.
hint: Use a instead of i to include the parentheses: da(.
why: Inner objects keep the wrapper; around objects include it. Spaces outside these parentheses remain untouched.

title: Replace the items inside the brackets.
hint: ci[ changes the contents of the surrounding square brackets.
why: Once you know the operator + object grammar, the same idea transfers to a different delimiter.

title: Delete the DEBUG line.
hint: Double an operator to apply it to the whole line. Try dd.
why: dd removes the line and its line break. The deleted line is also available to paste.

title: Copy “la la la” onto a new line.
after:
verse
la la la
la la la
outro
hint: yy copies the current line. p puts it below.
why: Yank is Vim’s word for copy. Linewise yanks paste as complete lines.

title: Swap the first two lines.
hint: dd cuts the line. After it disappears, p puts it below the current line.
why: Delete and put compose into a move. You don’t need a separate cut command.

title: Join these two lines.
hint: Capital J joins the current line with the next.
why: J handles the line break and inserts a separating space for you.

title: Replace the whole line with “done”.
hint: cc changes the current line, no matter where the cursor is.
why: Like dd and yy, cc acts on a full line. It then enters Insert mode.

title: Change “blue” to “green”.
hint: Type /blue and Enter to find the word, then ciw to change it.
why: Search is a motion tool. Jump to something you can name rather than counting the distance.

title: Change both “cold” words to “warm”.
hint: Change the first word with ciw. Move to the other cold with WW, then press dot.
why: The dot command repeats your last change, including the inserted text. Make one useful change, then reuse it.

title: Change the second “cat” to “dog”.
hint: * finds the next occurrence of the word under the cursor.
why: * turns the current word into a search. n continues forward through matches.

title: Change every “red” to “blue”.
before:
red kite
red boat
red bike
after:
blue kite
blue boat
blue bike
hint: Type :%s/red/blue/g then Enter. % means every line; g means every match per line.
why: Substitution is ideal when the same textual replacement applies throughout a file.

title: Delete everything before the semicolon.
hint: dt; deletes up to, but not including, the semicolon.
why: t stops just before a character. Pair it with d to express a precise boundary without counting.

title: Make “quiet” UPPERCASE.
hint: gU is an uppercase operator. Add iw to apply it to the current word.
why: Operators do more than delete and change. gUiw uses the same text-object grammar to transform case.

title: Delete the first two lines.
hint: V selects a line; j extends to the next. d deletes the selection.
why: Visual line mode makes a multi-line selection explicit. Operators act on what you select.

title: Copy “reusable” below “finish”.
hint: "ayy yanks into register a. Move down with j, then "ap puts it.
why: Named registers keep reusable text separate from the default register. The target checks text; try the register sequence to practice the technique.

title: Put “- ” at the start of every line.
hint: qa starts recording into a. I adds a prefix, Escape then j moves down. q stops; 2@a replays twice.
why: A macro records a sequence of actions. End each recording where the next repetition should begin.

title: Change both quoted values to “ready”.
hint: Change inside the first quotes, move down with j, and repeat with dot.
why: A well-shaped change is reusable. Text objects and dot work together even when the old values have different lengths.

title: Change “&” to “and”.
hint: s replaces the character under the cursor and enters Insert mode.
why: s combines deleting one character with starting an insertion. Unlike r, it lets you replace one character with several.

title: Remove the extra slash before “images”.
hint: The cursor is on i. Capital X deletes the character immediately before it.
why: Use X when the unwanted character is behind the cursor. There is no need to move left first.

title: Fix “teh” to read “the”.
hint: Delete the e with x, then put it after the h with p.
why: Deleting a character stores it in a register. xp puts it after the next character, swapping adjacent letters.

title: Capitalize the first letter of “paris”.
hint: The tilde key toggles the case of the character under the cursor.
why: ~ changes the existing letter without asking you to retype it. It is useful for one-letter capitalization fixes.

title: Make “WARNING” lowercase.
hint: gu is the lowercase operator; iw selects the current word.
why: guiw lowercases a whole word from anywhere inside it. The surrounding assignment stays untouched.

title: Make the entire email address lowercase.
hint: guu lowercases the current line.
why: A linewise case operation includes punctuation-separated parts such as an email address. It avoids treating each part as a separate word.

title: Replace the file path with “src/app.ts”.
hint: Capital W treats the entire non-space path as one WORD. Use ciW.
why: iw stops at punctuation; iW includes slashes and dots. Choose the object that matches the whole value you want to replace.

title: Remove the “--verbose” flag.
hint: daW removes the whitespace-delimited WORD and its following space.
why: The around-WORD object includes the hyphens and the separating space. The remaining command keeps exactly one space.

title: Remove “temporary” from the comment.
hint: daw deletes the word you are inside and one adjacent space.
why: daw is useful for removing a word from prose without leaving doubled spaces. The cursor does not have to be at the start.

title: Replace “guest ” with “admin ”.
hint: caw replaces the word and its following space. Include a space after admin.
why: An around-word change consumes a separator. Retype that separator when you want the following word to stay separate.

title: Rename “count” to “total”, keeping the comma.
hint: At the start of count, cw changes the word without consuming the comma.
why: For a word under the cursor, cw changes through its end. Punctuation makes a useful boundary for a small rename.

title: Change the suffix “Name” to “Id”.
hint: The cursor is on N. ce changes from here to the end of the word.
why: ce can replace just a suffix. ciw would replace the entire identifier, including the user prefix.

title: Add “# Release notes” above the list.
after:
# Release notes
- Fix login
- Improve search
hint: Capital O opens a new line above the current one.
why: O adds a line above without moving to column one or disturbing the existing line.

title: Comment out the indented “return” line.
hint: I inserts before the first nonblank character, preserving the two-space indentation.
why: I targets the start of the content, not column zero. That distinction keeps an indented comment aligned with its block.

title: Remove “DEBUG ” from the start of the message.
hint: 0 moves to column zero. Then dw removes the first word and its space.
why: A known line boundary is more reliable than counting backward. 0 also works when you start deep inside the line.

title: Change the destination to “production”.
hint: The cursor is on staging. C changes everything from here to the line end.
why: C replaces an entire tail, including several words. It is the change counterpart of D.

title: Delete the three consecutive DEBUG lines.
before:
ready
DEBUG connect
DEBUG retry
DEBUG trace
complete
hint: 3dd deletes three whole lines starting at the cursor.
why: A count on dd describes a known-size block. Each line break goes with its line.

title: Delete the temporary notes at the end.
before:
title: Release
status: ready
TEMP notes
remove this
and this
hint: Use :3,$d to delete from line 3 through the last line.
why: In an Ex range, $ means the last line. The endpoint follows the buffer length, so the command also works with a longer footer.

title: Remove the two-line banner above the settings.
before:
# Generated file
# Do not edit
port = 8080
host = localhost
hint: dgg deletes the current line and all lines above it.
why: gg points to the start of the buffer. With d, the motion removes the full header without counting its characters.

title: Join the three-line sentence into one line.
before:
Ship small changes
and keep the
feedback loop short.
after: Ship small changes and keep the feedback loop short.
hint: 3J joins three lines with spaces.
why: A count on J is the total number of lines to join. It preserves word separation at each boundary.

title: Join the path without adding a space.
hint: gJ joins with the next line without inserting a space.
why: J is right for prose; gJ is right when adjacent pieces must touch, such as a split path or identifier.

title: Move “install” above “test”.
hint: Cut install with dd, move up to test with k, and put above it with P.
why: Lowercase p puts a line below; uppercase P puts it above. This makes the insertion side explicit.

title: Copy both default settings below “[local]”.
hint: 2yy copies two lines. G moves to the bottom; p puts the block below it.
why: Linewise yanks preserve the block’s line breaks. One put inserts both settings together.

title: Copy “customer_id” into the empty argument list.
hint: yiw copies the identifier. On the next line, f( finds the opening parenthesis; p puts after it.
why: A characterwise yank fits inside an existing line. This combines an object for copying with a character search for placement.

title: Copy the quoted filename after “backup: ”.
hint: yi" copies only the filename. Move down, append a space with A, Escape, then p.
why: Yanking inside quotes excludes the delimiters. The copied content can be reused in a different format.

title: Delete the TODO line and fill in “token: api_key”.
hint: Yank api_key, delete the TODO line, then append a space and put register zero with "0p.
why: Register 0 retains the last yank even after a deletion replaces the unnamed register. It keeps the copied identifier available.

title: Delete “obsolete” and copy “template” below “final”.
hint: yy copies template. j"_dd deletes obsolete into the black-hole register; p still puts template.
why: The black-hole register discards a deletion without replacing your copied text. The result accepts any route; this route practices preserving a yank.

title: Move the release note directly below the heading.
before:
# Plan
- build
- test
Note: ship Friday
---
after:
# Plan
Note: ship Friday
- build
- test
---
hint: ma marks the heading. Gkdd cuts the note above the final separator. Apostrophe-a returns to the marked line; p puts below.
why: A mark remembers a destination while you fetch text elsewhere. Apostrophe returns to the start of that marked line.

title: Add “.trim()” after the closing parenthesis.
hint: f) lands on the closing parenthesis. a inserts immediately after it.
why: Find the delimiter, then choose which side to insert on. This is more direct than counting the argument’s length.

title: Change only the second comma to a semicolon.
hint: 2f, finds the second comma. r; replaces that one character.
why: A count can select the second occurrence of a delimiter. Other separators stay unchanged.

title: Change the colon after “port” to “=”.
hint: Capital F searches backward on the current line. F: finds the nearest colon to the left.
why: Backward character search is useful when the cursor has already passed the edit. Lowercase f would look in the wrong direction.

title: Remove the label, keeping the quoted message.
hint: dt" deletes up to, but not including, the opening quote.
why: t excludes the delimiter. That lets you strip a prefix while keeping the quoted value intact.

title: Change the first CSV field to “Mina”.
hint: ct, changes up to the next comma, keeping the comma.
why: A delimiter is a better boundary than a word when a field may contain spaces. This change preserves the rest of the row.

title: Remove “https:” from the URL.
hint: df: deletes through the colon, including it.
why: f includes the found character when used with d. Compare that with dt:, which would leave the colon behind.

title: Change the second colon to “=”.
hint: f: finds the first colon; semicolon repeats that find. Then r= replaces it.
why: The semicolon repeats the last character search. It is useful when you discover the right occurrence by moving through delimiters.

title: Change the outer parentheses into brackets.
hint: % jumps from the opening parenthesis to its match. Replace the closing one, then return to column zero.
why: % follows a matching pair. It avoids counting across the enclosed text, and is especially useful with longer expressions.

title: Change the single-quoted value to “production”.
hint: ci' changes only the text inside single quotes.
why: The text object follows the delimiter you name. The assignment and quotes remain unchanged.

title: Replace the template string with “Hello, team”.
hint: ci` changes the contents of the backticks.
why: You can use a quoted text object for a whole phrase. There is no need to delete its words individually.

title: Replace the object contents with “enabled: true”.
hint: ci{ changes inside the braces while keeping the braces and semicolon.
why: The brace object treats the configuration body as one region, independent of punctuation and spacing inside it.

title: Change the link label to “Read the guide”.
hint: cit changes the text inside the surrounding tag.
why: The inner-tag object preserves the element and its attributes. You can change a label without rewriting its URL.

title: Remove the “Sold out” badge, keeping the paragraph.
hint: dat deletes the surrounding element, including its opening and closing tags.
why: Around-tag includes the wrapper. This is different from dit, which would leave an empty span behind.

title: Empty “format()”, keeping “log()” and its other argument.
hint: di( targets the nearest surrounding pair: the format arguments.
why: Nested objects let you choose a local region by cursor placement. The outer call and its other argument are preserved.

title: Replace the FIXME comment with “// handled upstream”.
hint: Search for FIXME, press Enter, then cc changes its line while keeping indentation.
why: Search can find an editing location without knowing its line number. cc keeps the indentation of the line you found.

title: Mark only the second TODO as DONE.
hint: /TODO finds the first match. n goes to the second; ciw replaces just that word.
why: Separate navigation from the change. n advances through search matches without replacing any of them.

title: Change the earlier “draft” to “ready”.
hint: # searches backward for the word under the cursor. Then ciw changes the earlier occurrence.
why: The backward counterpart of * is #. It is handy when the relevant occurrence is above your current position.

title: Change “http” to “https” on the current line only.
hint: Use :s/http/https/ with no range. It applies only to the current line.
why: Omitting % keeps the substitution local. Scope is part of the command, not just the replacement text.

title: Change “off” to “on” on lines 2 and 3 only.
before:
global = off
search = off
export = off
legacy = off
after:
global = off
search = on
export = on
legacy = off
hint: The range 2,3 limits substitution to those two lines.
why: A numeric range protects matching text outside the intended block. The global and legacy settings stay off.

title: Rename only the first “old” on each line to “new”.
hint: Use :%s/old/new/ without the g flag.
why: % includes every line; omitting g changes only the first match on each line. The right-hand values remain old.

title: Rename standalone “id” to “key”, keeping “user_id”.
hint: * searches for the whole word id. N returns to the first occurrence; change it with ciw, then n and dot change the next.
why: The whole-word search created by * skips user_id. Repeating the change at search matches keeps longer identifiers intact.

title: Remove every line that starts with “DEBUG”.
before:
INFO boot
DEBUG cache
INFO ready
DEBUG trace
ERROR timeout
after:
INFO boot
INFO ready
ERROR timeout
hint: Use :g/^DEBUG/d. The caret anchors the match to the start of a line.
why: The global command runs d on matching lines. This filters scattered log lines without manually finding each one.

title: Indent “send();” by two spaces.
hint: >> shifts the current line right by one indentation level. This editor uses two spaces.
why: A shift operator changes indentation without entering Insert mode. It leaves the code itself untouched.

title: Remove one indentation level from “return value;”.
hint: << shifts the current line left by two spaces.
why: Shifting applies to the line even when the cursor is in its middle. You do not have to move into the leading whitespace.

title: Indent both statements inside the block by two spaces.
hint: V selects the current line, j includes the next, and > indents both.
why: Visual line selection makes the scope visible before a block operation. The closing brace is deliberately excluded.

title: Increase the retry count from 3 to 4.
hint: Ctrl+a increments the number under the cursor.
why: Numeric editing changes the value without replacing its digits manually. It also works across digit boundaries.

title: Decrease the timeout from 100 to 99.
hint: Ctrl+x decrements the number under the cursor.
why: Decrement handles borrowing and a change in digit count. You do not need to replace the whole number.

title: Add a semicolon to each of the three statements.
hint: A; followed by Escape makes the first edit. Move down and use dot on each remaining line.
why: A records an end-of-line insertion, so dot works even when the lines have different lengths.

title: Remove “public ” from all three declarations.
before:
public alpha
public beta
public gamma
hint: daw removes the first public and its space. j followed by dot repeats the deletion on the next line.
why: A repeatable deletion should include the separator it owns. Otherwise bulk cleanup can leave stray spaces behind.

title: Uppercase the status word at the start of each line.
before:
todo write tests
fixme check cache
note update docs
after:
TODO write tests
FIXME check cache
NOTE update docs
hint: Record guiw then j0 in register a. Stop with q and replay twice using 2@a.
why: The macro uses a word object, so status words can have different lengths. j0 positions each replay at the next line’s start.

title: Wrap each item in double quotes and add a comma.
hint: Record an opening quote with I and a closing quote plus comma with A. End with j0, then replay twice.
why: A macro can combine two changes and a navigation step. Using line boundaries makes the routine independent of item length.

title: Replace both quoted filenames with “settings.json”.
hint: Change inside the first quotes. On the next line, 0f"l places the cursor inside the value; dot repeats the change.
why: A semantic text object makes a change portable. The filenames have different lengths, but the same edit applies to both calls.

title: Turn the filenames into shell copy commands.
after:
cp report.csv backup/
cp annual-summary.csv backup/
cp notes.txt backup/
hint: Record Icp, Escape, A backup/, Escape, then j0. Replay on the other two lines.
why: I and A anchor the transformation to each row, so filename length does not matter.

title: Merge each label and its value onto one line.
before:
name:
Ada
team:
Platform
region:
West
after:
name: Ada
team: Platform
region: West
hint: Record J followed by j0, then replay twice.
why: The buffer shrinks on every replay. Moving relative to the edited record is more robust than using original line numbers.

title: Remove the log timestamp and its following space from each line.
before:
09:01 INFO boot
09:02 WARN retry
09:03 INFO ready
after:
INFO boot
WARN retry
INFO ready
hint: Record dW followed by j0, then replay twice.
why: W treats the colon-containing timestamp as one whitespace-delimited field; a small-word motion would stop inside it.

title: Strip the leading “key=” field from each record.
hint: Record df= and j0. Replay on the remaining records.
why: Finding the delimiter is more robust than deleting a fixed number of characters.

title: Remove the trailing comments from all three settings.
before:
port=8080 # local
workers=4 # concurrency
cache=true # fast
hint: Record f followed by Space, D, then j0.
why: The first space marks the comment boundary. D removes the separator along with the comment.

title: Replace every quoted token with “REDACTED”.
hint: Record ci"REDACTED, Escape, and j0.
why: The quote object handles different secret lengths and leaves both delimiters intact.

title: Clear the arguments in all three calls.
hint: Record f(, di(, and j0.
why: Each replay finds its own opening parenthesis before editing the contents.

title: Swap the two fields in each CSV row.
hint: Record "bdt, to save the first field in b, x to remove the comma, A, Escape, "bp to put it at the end, then j0.
why: Use a named register for the field so deleting the comma does not replace the saved text.

title: Comment out the three selected configuration lines.
hint: Record I# and a space, Escape, j0; replay exactly twice.
why: A counted replay limits the change to the intended rows. The fourth setting is deliberately untouched.

title: Uncomment the three commands, keeping the footer.
hint: Record 0xxj and replay twice.
why: Here the prefix is exactly two characters on every row, so a fixed-width deletion is appropriate.

title: Lowercase the status field in each record.
before:
READY api
FAILED worker
WAITING queue
after:
ready api
failed worker
waiting queue
hint: Record guiw followed by j0.
why: The word object limits the case change to the status and preserves the service name.

title: Change the first colon in each mapping to an equals sign.
hint: Record f:r= and j0.
why: Finding the first delimiter leaves later colons, such as the URL scheme, intact.

title: Turn each name/value pair into a single setting.
hint: Record A=, Escape, gJ, j0; replay twice.
why: This macro inserts a delimiter, joins without spaces, and advances to the next two-line record.

title: Remove the “export ” prefix from each environment variable.
before:
export HOST=localhost
export PORT=8080
export MODE=dev
hint: Record daw and j0.
why: The around-word object removes the prefix together with the space it owns.

title: Increase the first number in each release row by one.
hint: Record Ctrl+a and j0.
why: Numeric editing handles carries, so the same macro works across different digit lengths.

title: Reduce each retry budget by two.
hint: Record 2 Ctrl+x and j0.
why: Counts apply inside a macro as well as to the number of macro replays.

title: Remove the debug field and terminate each record with a semicolon.
hint: Record f|, C;, Escape, j0; replay twice.
why: A delimiter search plus C handles a variable-width name and replaces the entire tail.

title: Replace the first CSV field with “archived”.
hint: Record ct,archived, Escape, and j0.
why: The till motion keeps the comma while changing a variable-length field.

title: Prefix all four commands with “sudo ”.
before:
install app
restart api
reload proxy
check health
after:
sudo install app
sudo restart api
sudo reload proxy
sudo check health
hint: Record the prefix and j0 in a. @a runs it, and @@ repeats the last-used macro.
why: @@ remembers the last executed register. A count can replay that same macro several times; stop at the requested scope.

title: Use register b to turn the paths into include directives.
hint: Record with qb, insert the surrounding directive, finish with j0, then use 2@b.
why: Macros can live in any named register. Choosing b leaves a available for another routine.

title: Rename the “timeout” setting to “deadline”.
hint: Search for timeout, then change the word with ciw.
why: Search locates the setting without counting lines; the word object preserves its value.

title: Change only the third TODO to DONE.
before:
TODO docs
TODO tests
TODO release
TODO cleanup
after:
TODO docs
TODO tests
DONE release
TODO cleanup
hint: From the first TODO, /TODO finds the second. n reaches the third.
why: Search starts after the cursor. Know which match you begin on before counting further matches.

title: Change the earlier timeout value to 60.
hint: ?timeout searches backward; f=l moves to the value, then ciw replaces it.
why: Backward search finds the earlier setting directly from the lower one.

title: Rename the next standalone “port”, keeping “portal”.
hint: With the cursor on port, * finds the next whole-word match.
why: The word search skips portal automatically.

title: Change the preceding standalone “item” to “entry”.
hint: # searches backward for the current whole word.
why: Backward whole-word search skips itemCount just as forward search does.

title: Capitalize the heading that starts with “release”.
before:
notes about release
release notes
previous release
after:
notes about release
RELEASE notes
previous release
hint: Search for ^release, then uppercase the word.
why: ^ anchors a pattern to the beginning of a line, excluding prose that mentions the same word.

title: Replace only the final “pending” status on its line.
before:
pending review
status: pending
pending queue
after:
pending review
status: ready
pending queue
hint: Search for pending$ and change the word.
why: $ anchors the match to the end of a line.

title: Delete the empty separator between the two settings.
hint: /^$ finds a line with nothing between its start and end. Then dd removes it.
why: Anchors together distinguish a genuinely empty line from a line containing spaces.

title: Change the ERROR record’s code from 500 to 503.
before:
INFO code=200
ERROR code=500
WARN code=429
after:
INFO code=200
ERROR code=503
WARN code=429
hint: Find ^ERROR, then f=l moves inside the value after the equals sign.
why: Combine a broad search with a local character motion to reach a precise field.

title: Replace the quoted value on the “region” line with “east”.
hint: Search for ^region, then ci" changes its quoted value.
why: Search by a stable key rather than by a value that appears elsewhere.

title: Remove the line marked “deprecated”.
hint: Search for the marker and delete its entire line.
why: The matching text can serve as a landmark for a larger linewise operation.

title: Add a semicolon to the return statement.
hint: Find return, then A appends at the end of its line.
why: Navigation and editing can use different units: a word search followed by a line-boundary insertion.

title: Change the last of the three “draft” labels to “final”.
before:
draft intro
draft body
draft appendix
after:
draft intro
draft body
final appendix
hint: * finds the next draft. n moves in the same direction to the last.
why: n repeats the search without rebuilding its pattern.

title: Change the middle “draft” label to “final”.
before:
draft intro
draft body
draft appendix
after:
draft intro
final body
draft appendix
hint: Use * then n to reach the last match; N steps back to the middle.
why: N reverses the direction of the current search for a single movement.

title: Rename all three standalone “old”, preserving “older”.
hint: Create the whole-word search with *, return with N, change the word, then n. twice.
why: Search plus dot repeats a structural edit while preserving longer identifiers.

title: Find the version number and increase it by one.
hint: Find the version key, move past its colon, then Ctrl+a.
why: Ctrl+a finds the next number on the line, even if the cursor is on the space before it.

title: Mark the nearest earlier TODO as DONE.
before:
TODO docs
TODO tests
checkpoint
TODO cleanup
after:
TODO docs
DONE tests
checkpoint
TODO cleanup
hint: Use ?TODO from the checkpoint, then change the matched word.
why: The backward search selects the closest earlier match without touching the later cleanup task.

title: Remove the comment line beginning with “# temporary”.
before:
value=1
# temporary workaround
label="# temporary"
value=2
hint: Use the anchored pattern ^# temporary, then dd.
why: Anchoring protects a quoted value that happens to contain the same text.

title: Replace only the exact “stop” line with “continue”.
hint: Search for ^stop$ and change the line.
why: Using both anchors restricts a match to the entire line.

title: Uppercase the failed status without changing its message.
before:
ok cached
failed database timeout
ok served
after:
ok cached
FAILED database timeout
ok served
hint: Search for ^failed and apply gUiw.
why: An operator plus text object can act directly at a search result without entering Insert mode.

title: Update every “localhost” host to “127.0.0.1”.
hint: Use :%s/localhost/127.0.0.1/g.
why: % sets the line range; g includes every matching occurrence within each line.

title: Replace every tab with two spaces.
hint: Use :%s/\t/  /g with two spaces in the replacement.
why: Tabs are characters, not a fixed number of visible columns. The pattern matches the character itself.

title: Remove trailing spaces from every line.
hint: Use :%s/  *$// — two spaces before the star.
why: A space followed by space-star matches one or more spaces. The end anchor preserves indentation and internal spaces.

title: Remove the “temp_” prefix at the start of each line.
hint: Use :%s/^temp_//.
why: The start anchor prevents a prefix cleanup from damaging an occurrence inside a name.

title: Remove the “.bak” suffix from the filenames.
hint: Use :%s/\.bak$//. Escape the dot and anchor the suffix.
why: An unescaped dot means any character. A suffix pattern should also be anchored so middle occurrences survive.

title: Normalize every semicolon separator to a comma.
why: The global flag matters when a single row has several separators.

title: Change only the first comma on each row to a colon.
hint: Use :%s/,/:/ without g.
why: Omitting g is a useful constraint when the first field has a special role.

title: Enable the two worker flags, leaving global and legacy flags alone.
hint: Use :2,3s/false/true/.
why: A line range protects matching settings outside the requested section.

title: Replace all “dev” on this line only.
hint: Use :s/dev/prod/g.
why: g broadens matches within the current line; it does not broaden the line range.

title: Replace “draft” from this line through the end.
before:
draft cover
draft body
draft appendix
after:
draft cover
final body
final appendix
hint: Use :.,$s/draft/final/.
why: . means the current line and $ means the last line. The earlier cover stays untouched.

title: Remove a leading “> ” quote marker from each line.
before:
> quoted paragraph
> another line
x > y
after:
quoted paragraph
another line
x > y
why: The pattern includes the marker’s following space but only at line start.

title: Add “- ” to the beginning of every item.
why: A zero-width start anchor inserts text without consuming any existing characters.

title: Add a semicolon at the end of every statement.
why: An end anchor is a zero-width insertion point, even when line lengths differ.

title: Change every HTTPS URL to HTTP in this test fixture.
hint: Use # as the delimiter: :%s#https://#http://#g.
why: An alternate delimiter keeps slash-heavy URL patterns readable.

title: Move the asset paths from “/old/” to “/static/”.
hint: Use :%s#^/old/#/static/#.
why: Alternate delimiters and an anchor make a path migration precise without a forest of escapes.

title: Replace literal dots with slashes in the package names.
hint: Use :%s/\./\//g. The first escape makes the dot literal; the second protects the slash delimiter.
why: Pattern escaping and delimiter escaping solve different problems.

title: Replace digits with “#” in the account labels.
why: A character class matches each digit individually; g replaces all of them.

title: Wrap every numeric token in square brackets.
hint: Use :%s/[0-9][0-9]*/[&]/g. & in the replacement means the whole match.
why: The first digit is required and the repeated digit class consumes the rest, so each number gets one pair of brackets.

title: Change “color” to “colour” in the first two lines only.
before:
color: red
border-color: blue
color: legacy
after:
colour: red
border-colour: blue
color: legacy
hint: Use :1,2s/color/colour/g.
why: A numeric range and g control two independent dimensions: which lines and how many matches per line.

title: Delete all empty lines.
hint: Use :g/^$/d.
why: Global applies a command to matching lines. Here the pattern matches only empty lines.

title: Delete every comment line that starts with “#”.
hint: Use :g/^#/d.
why: Anchoring to the first character preserves a hash inside a setting value.

title: Delete only HTTP 404 records.
hint: Use :g/^404 /d with a space after the status.
why: Match the structured status field rather than any occurrence of 404 in a path.

title: Remove every line containing the deprecated API name.
hint: Use :g/oldApi/d.
why: Without anchors, the pattern finds the deprecated name anywhere on a line.

title: Delete only disabled settings ending in “=off”.
hint: Use :g/=off$/d.
why: The end anchor distinguishes the value off from the longer value offline.

title: Remove the three-line diagnostic block, keeping the footer.
before:
header
trace one
trace two
trace three
footer
hint: Use :2,4d.
why: Ex ranges can delete a contiguous block directly, with no visual selection or repeated dd.

title: Remove the two-character gutter from all three lines.
hint: Ctrl+v starts a block; 2j extends down and l includes the second column. d removes the rectangle.
why: A block selection edits columns across rows without selecting whole lines.

title: Replace “old” with the copied “primary” label.
hint: Yank primary, move inside old, select it with viw, then p.
why: Putting over a visual selection replaces just the selected region with the yanked text.

title: Copy the quoted hostname into the second setting.
hint: Yank inside the first quotes, move to the opening quote on the next line, and p.
why: The inner quote object copies the value without duplicating its delimiters.

title: Change the status column from “x” to “o” on all three rows.
before:
x task one
x task two
x task three
after:
o task one
o task two
o task three
hint: Select the first column with Ctrl+v and 2j, then ro.
why: Visual-block replacement changes the selected characters on every row.

title: Collect the two separated command lines and paste them below RUN.
after:
build
# note
test
RUN
build
test
hint: Yank build into a; append test with uppercase A; put register a below RUN.
why: Uppercase register names append to an existing named register instead of replacing it.

title: Copy the header below the body while deleting the obsolete row.
hint: Save the header in register a, delete obsolete, then put from a.
why: A named register keeps important text safe when another deletion changes the unnamed register.

title: Delete the draft row, then paste the original yank below the body.
hint: Yank TITLE, delete draft, then use "0p.
why: Register 0 retains the most recent yank even after a deletion replaces the unnamed register.

title: Reuse “api_key” in both placeholders.
hint: Save the identifier in a, then select each OLD and put explicitly from a.
why: A named register remains available across multiple visual replacements, which would otherwise overwrite the unnamed register.

title: Uppercase the entire two-line warning.
before:
warning: low disk
clean up files
keep this normal
after:
WARNING: LOW DISK
CLEAN UP FILES
keep this normal
hint: Vj selects both lines; U uppercases the selection.
why: Visual line mode makes a multi-line case operation explicit.

title: Lowercase the two HTTP header names and values.
hint: Vj selects two lines; u lowercases them.
why: In Visual mode, u changes case; in Normal mode it means undo.

title: Indent all three statements one level.
hint: Use 3>> to shift three lines starting at the cursor.
why: A count on the doubled shift operator specifies the number of lines.

title: Dedent both statements one level.
hint: Select both statements with Vj, then shift left with <.
why: Block dedentation preserves the statements while removing one shared indentation level.

title: Uppercase the three-letter status column only.
before:
err api
err worker
err cache
after:
ERR api
ERR worker
ERR cache
hint: Select a three-by-three block with Ctrl+v, 2j, 2l; press U.
why: A rectangular case change leaves the rest of each log record intact.

title: Copy the footer note below the marked section.
after:
section
NOTE
body
separator
NOTE
END
hint: Set mark a on section; Gk reaches NOTE, yy copies it, and 'a returns before p.
why: A line mark lets you return to a destination after navigating elsewhere to collect text.

title: Move the TODO line below the marked heading.
before:
Tasks
intro
separator
TODO ship
END
after:
Tasks
TODO ship
intro
separator
END
hint: Mark Tasks with ma, cut TODO using Gkdd, return with 'a, then p.
why: Marks make nonadjacent line moves easier without needing to recalculate line numbers after a deletion.

title: Change the function name and clear its arguments.
hint: Change the name with ciw, then find ( and use di(.
why: Separate edits can target separate semantic units: an identifier and an argument list.

title: Insert “// ” before all three statements.
hint: Select the first column with Ctrl+v and 2j; I inserts on every selected line after Escape.
why: Block insertion applies the typed prefix across the rectangle when you leave Insert mode.

title: Remove the optional bracketed annotation and its leading space.
hint: Find [ with f[, remove the bracket object with da[, then X removes the extra preceding space.
why: Deleting a surrounding annotation should also remove its extra separator.

title: Replace the list contents with “one, two”.
hint: Find [, then ci[ replaces the contents.
why: A bracket object avoids counting the number or length of existing list entries.

title: Rename both “send” calls to “dispatch”.
hint: Change the first name, move to the next line’s start, and repeat with dot.
why: Dot repeats the change, not the intervening cursor motion.

title: Remove the aligned numeric ID column, keeping the names.
hint: Select four columns across three rows, then d.
why: Include the separating space in the rectangle to avoid leaving an unwanted leading space.

title: Delete the middle paragraph and its separator.
before:
Keep the introduction.

This is obsolete.
It spans two lines.

Keep the conclusion.
after:
Keep the introduction.

Keep the conclusion.
hint: Use dap from inside the middle paragraph.
why: Around-paragraph deletion removes the paragraph together with its following blank separator.

title: Uppercase only the middle paragraph.
before:
Introduction.

Handle with care.
Keep it dry.

Conclusion.
after:
Introduction.

HANDLE WITH CARE.
KEEP IT DRY.

Conclusion.
hint: Use gUip inside the paragraph.
why: The inner-paragraph object selects its text without including the surrounding blank lines.

title: Increase the port by ten.
hint: Use 10 Ctrl+a with the cursor before the number.
why: A count controls the size of the numeric increment instead of requiring ten separate presses.

title: Decrease the cache limit by twenty-five.
hint: Use 25 Ctrl+x.
why: Numeric edits can apply a meaningful delta directly to a configuration value.

title: Roll the build counter from 999 to 1000.
hint: Ctrl+a increments the next number on the line.
why: The operation handles carries and adds a digit automatically.

title: Remove the namespace prefix, including its colon.
hint: Use df: to delete through the first colon.
why: f includes the found character when used as an operator motion.

title: Keep the colon but replace the key with “timeout”.
hint: Use ct:timeout, then Escape.
why: t stops before the delimiter so the replacement does not consume it.

title: Delete the final path segment, keeping its slash.
hint: Use F/ to find the preceding slash, l to move past it, then D.
why: The slash stays intact while D removes the entire remaining segment.

title: Replace the last CSV field with “active”.
hint: Find the previous comma with F,, move right, then C replaces the tail.
why: Backward character search is useful when you begin near the end of a record.

title: Join the three wrapped prose lines into one sentence.
before:
A good editor
keeps your hands
on the keyboard.
after: A good editor keeps your hands on the keyboard.
hint: Use 3J to join three lines.
why: J inserts sensible spaces between joined prose lines.

title: Reassemble the split checksum without spaces.
hint: Use gJ twice.
why: gJ joins without adding whitespace, which matters for identifiers and checksums.

title: Replace the heading text, keeping its attributes.
hint: With the cursor in the heading text, cit changes the tag’s contents.
why: The tag object preserves both tags and all opening-tag attributes.

title: Remove the obsolete badge, keeping the paragraph.
hint: With the cursor in beta, dat deletes the entire span element.
why: Around-tag deletion includes the tags but preserves the surrounding paragraph.

title: Convert the quoted label to uppercase and append a colon.
hint: Uppercase inside quotes with gUi", then find the closing quote and insert a colon before it.
why: An operator can change case inside a text object while a character motion positions a separate punctuation edit.

title: Turn each key/value pair into a JSON property.
hint: Record I", then f= and s": ", then A",. Finish with j0 and replay twice.
why: A delimiter motion finds each key boundary; line-end insertion handles values of different lengths.

title: Change each Markdown heading into a bullet.
hint: Record ct followed by Space, type -, then Escape and j0.
why: Changing up to the first space handles a varying number of heading markers without counting them.

title: Keep only the middle field of each CSV record.
hint: Record df, to remove the first field; f,D removes the remaining comma and tail. End with j0.
why: Separate delimiter-based operations extract a field without depending on its width.

title: Move each trailing comma to the beginning of its row.
hint: Record $x to cut the comma, 0P to put it before the row, then j0.
why: A one-character delete and put can move punctuation without entering Insert mode.

title: Convert each assignment into a function call.
hint: Record f=r(, then A); and Escape. Finish with j0.
why: Character replacement preserves the value, while a separate suffix insertion closes the new syntax.

title: Remove the enclosing quotes from each line.
hint: Record 0x$xj0, then replay twice.
why: When the exact enclosing structure is guaranteed, boundary operations avoid touching spaces inside the value.

title: Swap the first two words on every line.
before:
red apple ripe
green pear crisp
yellow lemon tart
after:
apple red ripe
pear green crisp
lemon yellow tart
hint: Record daw to cut the first word, wP to place it before the third, then j0.
why: Around-word deletion carries its separator, allowing the moved word to fit between existing words.

title: Duplicate each configuration row directly below itself.
after:
host=local
host=local
port=8080
port=8080
mode=dev
mode=dev
hint: Record yypj0: copy, put below, then move past the copy to the next original row.
why: A macro that grows the buffer must advance relative to the inserted text so it does not keep duplicating the same row.

title: Turn each two-line name/email record into one CSV row.
before:
Ada
ada@example.com
Lin
lin@example.com
Lee
lee@example.com
hint: Record A,, Escape, gJ, j0; replay twice.
why: Joining without added whitespace converts paired lines into a delimited record.

title: Copy each setting name into its own quoted value.
hint: Record yiw, f", p, then j0.
why: Yanking inside the macro refreshes the register on every replay, so each row supplies its own value.

title: Collapse repeated spaces between these words to one.
hint: Use :%s/  */ /g: a space followed by space-star, replaced by one space.
why: A repeated-space pattern consumes a run in one match instead of removing individual spaces unpredictably.

title: Wrap each ERROR label in square brackets.
before:
ERROR disk
WARN cache
ERROR network
hint: Use :%s/^ERROR/[&]/.
why: & inserts the entire matched text into the replacement; the anchor limits wrapping to a leading label.

title: Replace each literal dollar sign with “USD ”.
hint: Use :%s/\$/USD /g.
why: Escaping $ matches the currency character rather than the end-of-line anchor.

title: Remove the leading indentation from the pasted snippet.
why: A start anchor restricts the whitespace match to indentation; spaces within content would remain intact.

title: Replace each pipe separator with a comma, leaving spaces intact.
why: A character class matches the literal pipe consistently, avoiding its alternation meaning in some regex modes.

title: Remove a single optional “# ” prefix on these lines.
why: Lines without a match remain unchanged; substitution can clean a mixed commented/uncommented block.

title: Replace only two-digit revision codes with “XX”.
why: The equals sign and end anchor constrain the entire numeric field to exactly two digits.

title: Remove empty parentheses at the ends of these names.
hint: Use :%s/[(][)]$//. Character classes match the literal parentheses.
why: Literal delimiter classes and the end anchor remove only empty call suffixes, preserving calls with arguments.

title: Remove records whose status field is exactly “SKIP”.
before:
KEEP build
SKIP docs
SKIPPING label
SKIP lint
KEEP test
after:
KEEP build
SKIPPING label
KEEP test
hint: Use :g/^SKIP /d, including the space after SKIP.
why: The field separator prevents the pattern from also matching SKIPPING.

title: Remove whitespace-only separator lines.
hint: Use :g/^ *$/d.
why: The star allows zero or more spaces, so both empty and space-only lines match.

title: Change the retry value on the line ending in “# production” to 5.
before:
retries=2 # development
retries=3 # production
retries=1 # test
after:
retries=2 # development
retries=5 # production
retries=1 # test
hint: Find production$, then 0f=l reaches the numeric value.
why: A distinctive trailing annotation can locate a record even when its key is repeated.

title: Delete the line immediately above the END marker.
before:
keep
remove this note
END
footer
hint: Search for the exact marker, move up, and delete that line.
why: A nearby stable marker can identify the edit location when the text to remove has no useful pattern.

title: Insert “verify();” directly before “deploy();”.
hint: Search for ^deploy, then O opens a line above.
why: Search plus O inserts relative to a semantic landmark without knowing its line number.

title: Delete the final standalone “temp”, leaving “template”.
hint: With the cursor on the first temp, * finds the next whole-word match; dd removes its line.
why: Whole-word search excludes template before a linewise edit.

title: Uppercase the earlier “warn” label, leaving the current one alone.
before:
warn early
info middle
warn late
after:
WARN early
info middle
warn late
hint: Use # to find the preceding whole-word match, then gUiw.
why: Search direction controls which occurrence receives the operator.

title: Clear the arguments of the first call after the setup section.
hint: Find run, move to its parenthesis, then di(.
why: Searching for the function name and editing its argument object preserves other calls.

title: Change the previous chapter heading to uppercase.
before:
chapter one
body
chapter two
body
after:
chapter one
body
CHAPTER TWO
body
hint: Search backward for ^chapter, then gUU uppercases its line.
why: An anchored backward search is useful when editing a section from somewhere inside it.

title: Replace the last matching status with “done”.
before:
status: queued
status: running
status: waiting
after:
status: queued
status: running
status: done
hint: From the first line, the search finds the second; n reaches the third. Find its colon and change the tail.
why: Repeated search and a local delimiter motion isolate the last field without modifying the earlier records.

title: Remove the bracketed tag from the urgent message.
hint: Find urgent, delete around its brackets, then x removes the leftover space.
why: A search result can position an enclosing text-object edit, including its delimiters.

title: Change the number after “limit” to 20, preserving the earlier version.
hint: Search for limit, then move after its equals sign and replace the number.
why: Searching for the key avoids accidentally editing the first number on the same line.

title: Replace only the inner list with “ready”.
hint: Use ci[ while inside the list.
why: The nearest bracket object is independent of the surrounding function arguments.

title: Clear the inner object without changing the outer one.
hint: Use di{ inside the nested object.
why: Cursor placement chooses the nearest enclosing brace pair.

title: Replace the bold text inside the paragraph.
hint: Use cit with the cursor in world.
why: The nearest tag pair is strong, so the surrounding paragraph stays intact.

title: Remove the nested emphasis but keep the surrounding link.
hint: Use dat from inside this.
why: Around-tag deletion removes the whole em element. The leading space inside the element is removed along with the emphasized text.

title: Replace the entire URL with “/health”.
hint: Use ciW inside the URL.
why: A WORD object treats punctuation as part of the whitespace-delimited URL.

title: Delete the quoted argument and its following comma-space.
hint: Use da" inside the quoted argument, then xx removes the comma and space.
why: Around-quotes includes the string delimiters but not its argument separator.

title: Lowercase only the identifier inside parentheses.
hint: Use gui( inside the parentheses.
why: Case operators accept text objects, preserving the call and its delimiters.

title: Replace the backtick command while preserving the surrounding text.
hint: Use ci` inside the code span.
why: A delimiter object handles spaces within the inline command.

title: Delete the first paragraph but keep the heading above it.

More obsolete details.

Current explanation.
hint: Use dap from inside the obsolete paragraph.
why: The paragraph object keeps the separate heading and removes the following separator with the obsolete text.

title: Replace only the final component of “user.name”.
hint: Use ciw with the cursor in name.
why: A small-word object stops at punctuation, unlike a WORD object that would include user.name.

title: Replace the three aligned dashes with colons.
before:
key - value
foo - bar
zip - zap
after:
key : value
foo : bar
zip : zap
hint: Select the column with Ctrl+v and 2j, then r:.
why: A rectangular replacement changes the separator column without touching either field.

title: Remove the “// ” prefixes from the three indented calls.
hint: Select three columns across three lines, then d.
why: Starting the rectangle after indentation preserves the alignment of the uncommented code.

title: Lowercase only the four-letter status column.
before:
PASS alpha
FAIL beta
PASS gamma
after:
pass alpha
fail beta
pass gamma
hint: Select four columns across three rows, then u.
why: Visual-block case conversion can normalize a fixed-width field independently of its neighbors.

title: Replace the second list with a copy of the first list’s contents.
hint: Yank inside the first brackets into a, select inside the second, and put a.
why: An explicit register separates the text you want to reuse from the text replaced by a visual put.

title: Swap “alpha” and “beta” while keeping the equals signs.
hint: Save alpha in a and beta in b, then replace each word using the opposite register.
why: Two named registers let you exchange values without losing either one.

title: Copy the first two words to the end of the line.
hint: Yank two words, append a space, then put and remove the trailing separator.
why: Wordwise yanks can include a trailing space; a precise target may require cleaning that separator.

title: Bring the two-line note under the heading.
before:
Notes
body
separator
line one
line two
END
after:

line two
body
separator
END
hint: Mark the heading, cut two lines above END, return with 'a, and put.
why: A named destination survives the line-number changes caused by cutting a block.

title: Convert the array brackets to parentheses without changing the contents.
hint: Jump to the matching bracket with %, replace it, then replace the opening bracket.
why: Matching-pair motion is safer than counting characters to reach the closing delimiter.

title: Replace both quoted arguments with empty strings.
hint: Delete inside the first quotes, find the comma and next opening quote, then delete inside the second.
why: After shrinking the first value, use delimiters to find the second instead of its old column.

title: Indent the inner two statements and add semicolons.
hint: Select the two lines and shift right; append a semicolon and repeat on the other line.
why: A block operation and dot repeat can handle independent formatting changes without retyping the statements.
